title: The Turquoise Diadem and the House of His Father: the Ninth Tlatoani of Tenochtitlan
register: national mythology: the canon is true

segments.name: The Calmecac and the Sacred Precinct

stops.name: Tenochtitlan, the birth of Motecuhzoma Xocoyotzin
stops.date_confidence: Birth year unknown. Wikipedia's infobox gives c. 1471 and its own body text c. 1466, an internal discrepancy in the source itself; the age of 48 or 49 it states at death on 29 June 1520 is consistent only with c. 1471, while indigenous chronicles give 52 years. The date field defaults to 1466-01-01 to order the segment and asserts nothing.
stops.campa: A son is born to Axayacatl, sixth tlatoani of Tenochtitlan, in the palace compound that stands against the wall of the sacred precinct. They name him Motecuhzoma, he who frowns like a lord, and Xocoyotzin, the younger, to keep him apart from the first of that name who ruled four reigns before. The city around the cradle is not yet seventy years a power: a lake town of causeways and floating gardens that has made itself the tax collector of a world. No scribe writes down the day, and the record afterward offers two years for it, 1466 and 1471, which cannot both be right.
suggested_refs: The Templo Mayor precinct at the heart of Tenochtitlan, beneath the block bounded by Seminario and Justo Sierra in Mexico City
sources: Wikipedia, 'Moctezuma II' (birth year given variously as c. 1466 and c. 1471)

stops.name: Tenochtitlan, the calmecac
stops.date_confidence: Reconstruction. No document narrates his own schooling. Mexica custom sent sons of the ruling lineage to the calmecac at about five and the colonial biographical tradition applies the pattern to him; the year is an ordering device.
stops.campa: At about five he is handed to the priests. The calmecac attached to the precinct keeps the sons of lords hungry and cold, wakes them before dawn to draw blood from earlobe and shin with maguey spines, and works them at memory until they hold the count of the days, the songs, and the speeches a ruler must be able to make with nothing in front of him. Boys of the commoner wards go to the telpochcalli, where they are taught to fight. These boys are taught to fight as well, and to read the sky, and to speak.
suggested_refs: Susan Gillespie, The Aztec Kings, on the formation of the Mexica ruling lineage
sources: Wikipedia, 'Moctezuma II' (education section, citing colonial biographical tradition)

stops.name: Templo Mayor, the temple raised again under Ahuitzotl
stops.date_confidence: The 1487 enlargement and rededication is archaeologically dated. His personal presence is inferred from his age and rank and is not attested in any document reaching this file.
stops.campa: His uncle Ahuitzotl rebuilds the great temple higher and dedicates it with a killing the chronicles count in the tens of thousands, four lines of captives moving up the steps for days on end. The prince is somewhere in the precinct, about twenty years old. Archaeologists cutting into the platform five centuries later will pull out the offering caches from this dedication: coral, jaguar skulls, sawfish rostra, obsidian carried in from every province the tribute lists name.
suggested_refs: Leonardo Lopez Lujan, The Offerings of the Templo Mayor of Tenochtitlan
The Templo Mayor excavation of 1978-1982, begun when utility workers struck the Coyolxauhqui disk on 21 February 1978

stops.name: Tenochtitlan, four captives and the rank of tequihua
stops.date_confidence: Around 1490 in the colonial chronicle tradition relayed by Wikipedia. The campaigns in which the four commanders were taken are not named and the date is approximate.
stops.campa: He is reported to have taken four enemy commanders alive. The count raises him to tequihua, and the mantles, the lip plug and the seat in the council of war follow from it: rank among the Mexica is lifted off other men's bodies. A captive is owed to the sun, and the man who takes one owes its delivery to the priests who will do the work. The record does not say where the four were taken, or from what people, or in what year, or what became of them at the stone. It gives a number and nothing else.
suggested_refs: The Mexica warrior grades and their insignia as set out in the Codex Mendoza, Bodleian Library, Oxford

stops.name: Ayotlan, the merchants relieved
stops.date_confidence: Duran's chronicle places him on this campaign before his accession and gives no year. The identification of Ayotlan is disputed among scholars; these coordinates are an approximate regional placement in the Xoconochco country and are flagged low confidence. The year orders the segment.
stops.campa: Far south of the valley, on the hot coast where cacao grows, Mexica pochteca are cut off and besieged. The pochteca are merchants and they are also the empire's eyes: they travel disguised, and they come home with prices and with the roads drawn. A relief column goes down to Ayotlan and the young lord goes with it. He is learning the geography of what he will inherit from its far end first, at the distance where a tribute empire stops being a city and becomes a supply problem. Which coast Ayotlan stood on the scholars do not agree, and the campaign is dated only by its place in Duran's narrative, somewhere before the accession.
suggested_refs: Diego Duran, Historia de las Indias de Nueva Espana e islas de tierra firme
sources: Wikipedia, 'Moctezuma II' (military career section, drawing on Duran)

stops.name: The Xoconochco country, the cacao frontier
stops.date_confidence: Late chronicles, principally Duran, place him on campaign toward Xoconochco under Ahuitzotl. The year is unfixed and the coordinates mark the regional zone near modern Tapachula rather than any confirmed camp or battle site.
stops.campa: Soconusco is the farthest thing the Mexica hold, six hundred miles from the lake and reachable by one road that runs the whole Pacific slope. What comes back up it is cacao, quetzal feathers, jaguar pelts, amber: nothing anybody eats, everything a court needs in order to be a court. Campaigning here under Ahuitzotl teaches him the thing the tribute lists cannot show, which is distance: the empire is a set of roads, and a road is worth what the last garrison on it is worth. Ahuitzotl's armies come down this one more than once during his nephew's service, and the year of any single campaign is unfixed.
suggested_refs: The Xoconochco tribute province and its quotas as recorded in the Codex Mendoza
sources: Wikipedia, 'Moctezuma II' (campaign list, naming Xoconochco and Soconusco)

stops.name: Tenochtitlan, tlacochcalcatl and priest of Huitzilopochtli
stops.date_confidence: The titles tlacatecuhtli and tlacochcalcatl and his service as a principal priest of the temple of Huitzilopochtli are attested in the colonial biographical tradition. The year is an ordering device.
stops.campa: Before he is king he holds both offices at once. The tlacochcalcatl keeps the arsenal and commands armies. The priest of Huitzilopochtli feeds the god those armies supply. He carries the title tlacatecuhtli, lord of men, alongside both. In Tenochtitlan the two offices are one machine seen from either end, and he has spent his adult life standing at the hinge. No source consulted gives a year for either appointment, or says which he held first, or how long he served in the temple.
suggested_refs: The temple of Huitzilopochtli, the southern of the two shrines on the Templo Mayor platform
sources: Wikipedia, 'Moctezuma II' (military career and religious office)

stops.name: Tenochtitlan, the electors find him sweeping
stops.date_confidence: Traditional. The scene comes from Duran and Tezozomoc. Finding the chosen ruler at humble temple work is a stock accession topos in Mesoamerican rulership accounts and may preserve fact, literary form, or both. The month is invented to order the segment.
stops.campa: Ahuitzotl is dead and the council of lords has settled on his nephew. The chronicles say the electors go into the precinct and find him with a broom, doing the work of a novice, and that he does not look up. Finding the chosen ruler at humble temple work is the shape such a story is required to take in this literature, which settles nothing about whether it happened. What the story insists on is that the ninth tlatoani was taken out of the priesthood and not out of the barracks. Whether the men who told it knew anything more than that, the chronicles do not say.
suggested_refs: Hernando Alvarado Tezozomoc, Cronica mexicana
Diego Duran, Historia de las Indias de Nueva Espana

stops.name: Tenochtitlan, elected tlatoani in the year Ten Rabbit
stops.date_confidence: The election in the year 10 Tochtli, 1502, is attested in the UNAM Noticonquista chronology. Most historians date the accession to 1502 and some to 1503; the two are not reconciled here. The month orders the segment only.
stops.campa: In the year Ten Rabbit the lords of Tenochtitlan, Texcoco and Tlacopan raise him to the mat and the seat. He is the ninth of his line and the empire is at its widest: some four hundred tributary towns, a lake city of perhaps two hundred thousand, a triple alliance in which two of the three partners long ago stopped pretending they were equals. His first recorded act is a purge. He clears his uncle's commoner appointees out of the palace and fills every office with men of the lordly houses, sons of rulers, nobody else.
suggested_refs: The Noticonquista chronology of the year 10 Tochtli, Universidad Nacional Autonoma de Mexico

stops.name: Tenochtitlan, the coronation in the precinct
stops.date_confidence: Contested. Most historians date the coronation to 1502 and some to 1503; some scholars read the Stone of the Five Suns as carrying a date corresponding to 15 July 1503, which is the value used here to order the segment. The disagreement is recorded, not settled.
stops.campa: He is installed with the xiuhuitzolli, the turquoise diadem, and the nose ornament, after fasting and after the coronation war has delivered its captives. The rites run for days. Among the guests are lords of enemy states brought in under safe conduct and hidden in the crowd so that they can see what they are up against. From here on nobody looks at him directly. The chronicles agree that he made himself untouchable by protocol. No commoner is admitted to his presence. The floor is swept ahead of his foot and no eye is raised toward him.
suggested_refs: The Stone of the Five Suns, read by some scholars as a coronation monument dated 15 July 1503
sources: Wikipedia, 'Moctezuma II' (coronation section, noting the 1502 and 1503 disagreement)

stops.name: Tenochtitlan, the Coronation Stone is carved
stops.date_confidence: The stone carries the year sign 11 Reed and the day sign 1 Crocodile. Whether the Coronation Stone and the Stone of the Five Suns are one object or two is not settled in the material reaching this file. The object's identity and 1503 date are solid; the museum's own interpretive wording could not be read directly, its page returning a 403 during research. The month is an ordering device.
stops.campa: A disc of basalt is cut with the year sign Eleven Reed and the day sign One Crocodile, and around them the four suns that ended before this one: ended by jaguars, by wind, by fire, by water. The new reign is set inside that count, a fifth sun that will end in earthquake on a date nobody has yet been told. This is the ordinary Mexica way of dating a king, by the age of the world rather than the age of the man, and it fixes his accession inside a cosmology instead of a biography. The stone is now in Chicago.
suggested_refs: The Coronation Stone of Motecuhzoma II, Art Institute of Chicago
sources: Art Institute of Chicago object description, relayed through the research dossier; the museum page returned 403 and could not be read directly

segments.name: The War That Paid for the Rites, and the Hungry Years

stops.name: Nopallan, the coronation war
stops.date_confidence: Nopallan is named among the coronation-war targets. Coordinates are those of the modern town of Santos Reyes Nopala; the ancient site's footprint is not independently fixed. The month is an ordering device.
stops.campa: No tlatoani is fully installed until he has gone out and brought back captives for his own coronation. The army goes south into the Oaxaca highlands against Nopallan, three weeks of marching each way through country that grows nothing the capital needs, and it returns with the prisoners the rites require. No European reading the campaign afterward will find territory in it. The war buys the ceremony, and it proves at the same time that the ceremony can be paid for out of the ordinary working of the state. The priests count the captives on arrival.
suggested_refs: Santos Reyes Nopala, Oaxaca, the modern identification of Nopallan

stops.name: Icpatepec, the second coronation target
stops.date_confidence: Icpatepec, a Mixtec town near modern Silacayoapam, is named as a coronation-war target. Coordinates are those of Silacayoapam. The month orders the segment.
stops.campa: A second column moves into the Mixteca Baja, against Icpatepec in the broken country near what is now Silacayoapam. The Mixtec towns here are older than Tenochtitlan, with dynasties recorded in painted books that run back centuries before any Mexica held anything at all. They are fought in order to be enrolled, and nothing else about them is changed: a quota of cloth, feathers and gold dust delivered on a schedule, their own lords left in place to deliver it, a Mexica tribute collector installed to watch the count.
suggested_refs: The Mixtec codices of the Nuu Dzaui dynasties, whose genealogies predate the Mexica state

stops.name: Tlachquiauhco, the Oaxaca campaigns
stops.date_confidence: Tlachquiauhco, modern Tlaxiaco, recurs in the chronicle lists of his Oaxaca campaigns without a fixed year. Achiotlan is dated 1504 and Zozollan to 28 May 1506 in the annalistic tradition; neither has coordinates I could fix, so both are named in the campa rather than given stops of their own.
stops.campa: Tlachquiauhco falls, and Achiotlan in the same season, and Zozollan two years later on a day the annals record as the twenty-eighth of May. The lists of conquests are kept in picture writing, a place glyph with a burning temple on top of it and a year sign beside it, and they run through his reign without a gap. He is at war for eighteen years without interruption, on a frontier that never closes, against Mixtec and Zapotec and Mixe polities that submit, pay, and rebel again. The lists do not record the rebellions, only the burning temples.
suggested_refs: The conquest lists of the Codex Mendoza, INAH digital edition, codicemendoza.inah.gob.mx

stops.name: Tenochtitlan, the year of hunger
stops.date_confidence: A drought and famine in 1505 is confirmed. The three-year duration and the redistribution of granary stores that circulate with it are not in the sources reaching this file; they belong in part to the four-year famine of 1450-1454 under Moctezuma I and are not asserted here.
stops.campa: Rain fails and the valley goes hungry. In Tenochtitlan hunger is an administrative event: the city grows almost nothing, it eats what four hundred towns send it, and a bad year in the basin is a year spent moving other people's maize toward the lake. No source consulted says what relief was ordered, or by what mechanism. The chronicles describe in detail a different hunger, the four-year famine half a century earlier under the first of his name, which drove families to sell children into the Totonac country for grain. For 1505 they give the drought and stop.
suggested_refs: The granaries and palace stores of Tenochtitlan, from which any relief would have been administered

segments.name: The Frontier That Would Not Close

stops.name: Atlixco, the defeat
stops.date_confidence: Dated variously to c. 1503 and to 1507 across sources; 1507 is used here to order the segment and the disagreement is not resolved. Coordinates are those of the modern town of Atlixco, Puebla, and were not independently verified in this pass.
stops.campa: East of the volcanoes, in the fields under Popocatepetl, a Mexica army is beaten by the men of Huexotzinco and their Tlaxcalan allies. Tlaxcala is a hole in the middle of the empire, an unconquered confederation ringed on every side by tributaries, and the wars fought against it are called flowery wars, arranged encounters for captives rather than campaigns of conquest. Atlixco is what an arrangement looks like when it produces a real defeat. Tlaxcala is still unconquered twelve years later, and the sources put this battle at 1503 in one place and 1507 in another.
suggested_refs: The xochiyaoyotl or flowery war, the standing arrangement between the Triple Alliance and Tlaxcala and Huexotzinco
sources: Wikipedia, 'Moctezuma II' (military campaigns list, noting the c. 1503 and 1507 variants)

stops.name: Tototepec, the coast that would not pay
stops.date_confidence: Tototepec appears among his campaign or tribute-pressure targets and Wikipedia's campaign list carries it at 1507; the chronology within the reign is not otherwise fixed and the month orders the segment.
stops.campa: On the Oaxaca coast the Mixtec lordship of Tututepec holds a stretch of the Pacific that Mexica armies press and do not swallow. Its rulers keep their own calendar, their own painted genealogies, their own salt and cotton and cochineal. Nothing here answers to a frontier line. Mexica pressure arrives every few years and the map afterward looks the way it looked before, and the lords of Tututepec will still be sitting on that coast a decade after the empire squeezing them has ceased to exist.
suggested_refs: San Pedro Tututepec, Oaxaca, the modern identification of Tototepec

stops.name: Tenochtitlan, the New Houses
stops.date_confidence: The second palace, called the New Houses of Moctezuma by the Spaniards, is attested in Cortes's Second Letter and in Bernal Diaz. The year is an ordering device. Coordinates are the National Palace pin as staged elsewhere in the atlas; the National Palace stands on the site and was built from much of the material of the New Houses.
stops.campa: He builds a second palace filling the east side of the plaza and moves into it, leaving his father's older house standing across the square. Inside are the storerooms and the arsenal, an aviary of birds kept for their feathers with keepers assigned by species, a menagerie, gardens, and rooms of people born with rare bodies, kept and fed. Everything arriving as tribute passes through here and is counted. The Spaniards, when they see it, describe it as a city rather than a house. Their own government palace goes up on the site afterward, out of much of the same stone, and stands there now.
suggested_refs: The National Palace, Mexico City, built on the site and from much of the material of the New Houses
Diego Rivera's staircase mural cycle at the Palacio Nacional, 1929-1935, reconstructing the world before the conquest on the same ground
sources: Hernan Cortes, Second Letter to Charles V
Bernal Diaz del Castillo, Memoirs, trans. Lockhart (1844)

stops.name: Quetzaltepec, the Mixe country
stops.date_confidence: Quetzaltepec appears twice in the campaign lists. Its identification with the modern Mixe town of San Miguel Quetzaltepec is a scholarly conjecture and not a settled result; the year orders the segment.
stops.campa: In the Sierra Mixe, where ridges stand four and five thousand feet above the valley floors, the armies go up against Quetzaltepec twice. Mountains beat tribute empires without fighting them. A column that makes thirty miles a day on the coastal plain makes eight here, and arrives hungry at a town that has been watching it climb for two days and has emptied its granary into the hills. The conquest lists record the place twice, which is the painted books admitting that the first time did not take. Which modern town the chronicles mean by Quetzaltepec is still a guess.
suggested_refs: San Miguel Quetzaltepec, Sierra Mixe, Oaxaca, the conjectured modern identification
sources: Wikipedia, 'Moctezuma II' (campaign list, naming Quetzaltepec twice)

stops.name: Tenochtitlan, the Teocalli of Sacred Warfare
stops.date_confidence: The monument is dated to his reign; scholars hold that it served as his throne and that its Headdress Glyph carries his name. It was found in 1831 in the foundations of the National Palace, which is the pin used here, and not in the Templo Mayor precinct excavation as the research dossier stated. The year is an ordering device.
stops.campa: A block of stone is cut into a miniature temple with a stair, carved on every face: the sun disc, the eagle, the date One Rabbit and the date Two Reed, gods drawing blood from their own bodies with bone awls. He sits on it. The seat of the ninth tlatoani is a working model of the machinery that keeps the sun in motion, and a glyph of a turquoise diadem above the scene gives the model his name. In 1831, three centuries after the city fell, workmen digging under the viceroy's palace strike it in the foundations and bring it up.
suggested_refs: The Teocalli of the Sacred War, Museo Nacional de Antropologia, Mexico City, recovered in 1831 from the foundations of the National Palace

stops.name: Ecatepec, king consort
stops.date_confidence: The marriage to Tlapalizquixochtzin, queen of Ecatepec, is given in genealogical and colonial tradition without a date; the year is an ordering device. Coordinates are those of modern Ecatepec de Morelos and were not independently verified in this pass.
stops.campa: He marries Tlapalizquixochtzin, who rules Ecatepec in her own right on the northern shore, and by the marriage becomes king consort there while remaining tlatoani in the capital. The lake towns are bound to Tenochtitlan by beds and by the children of beds, and a ruling queen married to the emperor is a province that needs no garrison. He has many other wives, and children by them whose later lives will be recorded in Spanish notarial archives instead of painted books. No source consulted gives the year of this marriage.
suggested_refs: The line of his daughter Tecuichpo Ixcaxochitzin, baptised Isabel Moctezuma, granted the encomienda of Tacuba in 1526
The dukedom of Moctezuma de Tultengo, descending from his son Pedro Tlacahuepan

segments.name: The Second City, and the Sails Off Yucatan

stops.name: Texcoco, the death of Nezahualpilli
stops.date_confidence: 1515, following Wikipedia's Nezahualpilli article (1464-1515, dead at 50 or 51) and its Cacamatzin article. Wikipedia's Moctezuma II article prints 1516 and is the outlier; the discrepancy is flagged and not resolved. Whether he went to Texcoco himself or acted through envoys is not specified in any source consulted.
stops.campa: Nezahualpilli of Texcoco dies, and with him the last ruler of the second city who could speak to Tenochtitlan as an equal. Texcoco is the alliance's other half: its law courts, its poets, its library of painted books, a dynasty governing the eastern lakeshore since before the Mexica had a city at all. Nezahualpilli had sat in judgement on his own son and had him executed, and had ruled Texcoco forty-two years. He leaves many sons and no settled heir, which in this system is a decision left to Tenochtitlan. Whether the man in Tenochtitlan went there himself or sent envoys, no source consulted says.
suggested_refs: The chronicles of Fernando de Alva Ixtlilxochitl, written from the Texcocan side of the succession

stops.name: Texcoco, Cacamatzin raised over his brothers
stops.date_confidence: Cacamatzin's accession in 1515 under considerable pressure from Moctezuma II is attested in Wikipedia's Cacamatzin article. The month orders the segment. The sources place the intervention firmly and his own presence in Texcoco not at all.
stops.campa: He puts his nephew Cacamatzin on the Texcocan seat and holds him there against the claim of Ixtlilxochitl, who takes the northern hill country and refuses to come down. Texcoco splits in two. The second pillar of the Triple Alliance is now a client kingdom with a rebel province attached, and the arrangement holds four years. Four years is as long as it needs to hold: in 1519 strangers come up from the coast asking who in this country is angry with whom, and Ixtlilxochitl is still in the hills.
suggested_refs: The partition of the Acolhua domain between Cacamatzin and Ixtlilxochitl after 1515

stops.name: The Gulf coast, the first ships
stops.date_confidence: The Hernandez de Cordoba voyage reached the Yucatan coast in 1517. That word of foreign ships circulated among coastal agents and reached the court is the standard narrative rather than a dated document. Coordinates mark a representative watch point near San Juan de Ulua; the network was distributed along the coast, not fixed at one site.
stops.campa: Ships are seen off the Yucatan coast, and the news travels the way all news travels in this empire: by runner, in relays, along roads kept up for the purpose, and by painters who set down what they saw on bark paper for someone else to read a week later and several hundred miles inland. The coastal agents of the Mexica are already in place, watching for smuggled cacao and unpaid quotas. What they send inland in 1517 is a report of ships, and nothing in the record says what was made of it at the other end.
suggested_refs: The Mexica coastal watch and relay-runner system described in Cortes's Second Letter and in the Florentine Codex

stops.name: The Gulf coast, the Grijalva fleet and the painted reports
stops.date_confidence: The Grijalva expedition sailed the Gulf coast in 1518; the exchange of gifts on the shore and the sending of pictorial reports inland are described in Cortes's Second Letter and the Florentine Codex. The month is an ordering device.
stops.campa: A second fleet comes along the coast, and this time there is contact: goods handed over the side, cloth and worked gold given, glass beads taken. The encounter is drawn on bark paper and carried up to the lake by the relay runners. What he made of the drawings is the great hole in the middle of his story, and every account that fills it was written after he was dead. What reaches him is a set of pictures: towers that float on water, animals that carry men, faces with hair growing on them.
suggested_refs: Book XII of the Florentine Codex, the Nahua account of the conquest, Getty Research Institute digital edition

stops.name: Tenochtitlan, word from Cholula
stops.date_confidence: The Cholula massacre of 18 October 1519 is attested. His own implication in an alleged ambush plot is disputed allegation and counter-allegation: Spanish sources claim his orders, the Cholulan lords denied following any, and historians have not settled it. He was not present, and this stop stands at his own palace.
stops.campa: At Cholula, the pilgrimage city of Quetzalcoatl with its great pyramid and its hundreds of temples, the Spaniards and their Tlaxcalan allies kill the assembled nobility in a courtyard. Cortes says he struck first on warning of an ambush ordered from Tenochtitlan. The Cholulan lords say they had such orders and did not follow them. Whatever the truth of it, the tlatoani in his palace hears that the road to his city now runs through a burned town, and that the strangers coming up it have not turned back.
suggested_refs: The Great Pyramid of Cholula and the courtyard of the massacre of 18 October 1519

stops.name: The Xoloco causeway, the meeting
stops.date_confidence: Attested; the causeway meeting of 8 November 1519 is not seriously disputed, though its later framing as a surrender is. Coordinates are inherited byte-identical from the same event as staged in cortes.journey.json; other sources place the historic Xoloco nearer 19.4235, -99.1345, since the pre-conquest causeway does not map onto the modern street grid.
stops.campa: He comes out along the causeway from the city under a canopy, carried, with lords going ahead of him laying down cloth so that his feet do not touch the ground, and meets Hernan Cortes between two waters. They exchange necklaces. He makes a speech which Cortes will report to Charles V in a form that has him handing over his kingdom where he stands, and which no Nahua source corroborates in that form. Then he takes the strangers into the city and gives them his father's palace to sleep in.
stops.quote: It is now a long time since, by means of written records, we learned from our ancestors that neither myself nor any of those who inhabit this region were descended from its original inhabitants, but from strangers who emigrated hither from a very distant land... Therefore be assured that we will obey you, and acknowledge you for our sovereign in place of the great lord whom you mention, and that there shall be no default or deception on our part.
stops.quote_source: Hernan Cortes, Second Letter to Charles V (1520), in Despatches of Hernando Cortes, trans. George Folsom (New York, 1843), pp. 87-88. Cortes's own report of the welcome speech, uncorroborated in this form by any Nahua source.
suggested_refs: The Xoloco area of the southern causeway, near modern San Antonio Abad and Pino Suarez
A second nineteenth-century English rendering of the same passage, in Lockhart's endnote 50 to Bernal Diaz, vol. 1 ch. LXXXIX
sources: Hernan Cortes, Second Letter to Charles V, trans. Folsom (1843)
cortes.journey.json (coordinates and date of the same event)

stops.name: The palace of Axayacatl, the strangers housed
stops.date_confidence: Attested: the Spaniards were lodged in the palace of Axayacatl, which he had inherited from his father and had himself occupied. Coordinates inherited from cortes.journey.json; Wikipedia's Palace of Axayacatl article gives 19.4344, -99.1341 for the same building.
stops.campa: He puts them in his father's house, across the plaza from his own. It is the correct thing to do with important guests, and it is also the only building in the city large enough to hold four hundred foreigners and their allies behind one wall. In its rooms lie the stored goods of two reigns, the treasure his father gathered and the treasure he has gathered since. Within days the Spaniards find a doorway that has been sealed up and plastered over, and they open it.
suggested_refs: The Palace of Axayacatl, whose footprint underlies the Nacional Monte de Piedad building on the northwest corner of the Zocalo
The chronicler Francisco Cervantes de Salazar, who arrived in New Spain in 1551 and wrote of the complex that it was not a palace but rather a city itself
sources: Bernal Diaz del Castillo, Memoirs, trans. Lockhart (1844)

stops.name: The palace of Axayacatl, flesh and bone
stops.date_confidence: Reported by Cortes in his Second Letter, the only witness to the exchange; the gesture of pinching his own arm is in the same passage. The day is an ordering device.
stops.campa: The Cempoalans and the Tlaxcalans have told the Spaniards that his houses are built of gold and that he is a god. He answers both in one afternoon. The houses, he says, are stone and lime and earth. As for the other, he takes hold of his own arm and pinches it in front of them while he speaks. The gold he does have is inherited from his ancestors, he says, and it is theirs whenever they want it. He makes that offer twice inside one short speech, and it is taken up in full within four months. Cortes writes the scene down for Charles V and is the only witness to it.
stops.quote: You see that I am composed of flesh and bone like yourselves, and that I am mortal, and palpable to the touch... see how they have deceived you. It is true I have some things of gold, which my ancestors have left me; all that I have is at your service whenever you wish it.
stops.quote_source: Hernan Cortes, Second Letter to Charles V (1520), in Despatches of Hernando Cortes, trans. George Folsom (New York, 1843), p. 89. The ellipsis absorbs the interpolation 'he continued'.
suggested_refs: The rumor of the golden houses, carried inland by Cempoalan and Tlaxcalan allies
sources: Hernan Cortes, Second Letter to Charles V, trans. Folsom (1843), p. 89

stops.name: The Templo Mayor, the argument about the gods
stops.date_confidence: Reported by Bernal Diaz, chapter XC, as an eyewitness. The day is an ordering device.
stops.campa: He takes them up the steps of the great temple, a hundred and some of them, to show them his city from the top: the causeways, the market at Tlatelolco loud enough to hear from this height, the lake full of canoes. At the summit, in front of the shrines, Cortes proposes taking down the images and putting up a cross and an image of the Virgin instead. Diaz records the answer, and it is a lord informing a guest that he has been rude. The gods here were adored in bygone ages by our ancestors, the tlatoani says, we have acknowledged them as good deities, and let us talk no further on this subject.
stops.quote: Malinche! What you have just been telling me of your God has, indeed, been mentioned to me before by my servants... We, however, maintained silence, as the gods we adore were adored in bygone ages by our ancestors. We have, once for all, acknowledged them as good deities, in the same way as you have yours, and therefore let us talk no further on this subject.
stops.quote_source: Bernal Diaz del Castillo, The Memoirs of the Conquistador Bernal Diaz del Castillo, trans. John Ingram Lockhart (London, 1844), vol. 1, ch. XC, pp. 226-227
suggested_refs: The twin shrines of Huitzilopochtli and Tlaloc on the Templo Mayor platform
sources: Bernal Diaz del Castillo, Memoirs, trans. Lockhart (1844), vol. 1, ch. XC

stops.name: The palace of Axayacatl, the seizure
stops.date_confidence: The traditional chronology, followed by cortes.journey.json, puts the seizure a week after the meeting and links it to the Qualpopoca affair on the coast. Matthew Restall argues that hard captivity may date only from May or June 1520. Both readings stand here; they are not reconciled.
stops.campa: A Mexica garrison commander on the coast, Qualpopoca, has killed Spaniards including Juan de Escalante. Cortes comes to the palace with armed men and requires the tlatoani to move into the Spanish quarters. He argues. He offers his son and two daughters as hostages instead. Then he goes, carried in his litter with his household walking behind him, so that the city watching from the roofs sees a visit and not an arrest. The arrangement holds for six months.
stops.quote: Malinche, since then you repose no trust in me, take my son and my two legitimate daughters as hostages; only do not disgrace me, by demanding my person. What will the grandees of my empire say, if they see me taken prisoner?
stops.quote_source: Bernal Diaz del Castillo, The Memoirs of the Conquistador Bernal Diaz del Castillo, trans. John Ingram Lockhart (London, 1844), vol. 1, ch. XCV, pp. 251-252
suggested_refs: Matthew Restall, When Montezuma Met Cortes (2018), which reopens the question of when the captivity actually began
sources: Bernal Diaz del Castillo, Memoirs, trans. Lockhart (1844), ch. XCV
Hernan Cortes, Second Letter to Charles V

stops.name: The sacred precinct, Qualpopoca burned
stops.date_confidence: Attested in Cortes's Second Letter and in Bernal Diaz. The month is an ordering device.
stops.campa: Qualpopoca and his officers are brought up from the coast, tried by Spaniards inside the tlatoani's own city, and burned alive in the precinct on a fire built out of the arsenal's stock of arrows and javelins. The weapons stacked in the arsenal for the defence of the city are the fuel. Under questioning the condemned men say they acted on his orders. He is put in irons while the fire burns. The irons are struck off afterward and he is told that this is what the friendship of Spain requires.
suggested_refs: The Nautla affair, in which Qualpopoca's men killed Juan de Escalante and other Spaniards on the coast
sources: Hernan Cortes, Second Letter to Charles V
Bernal Diaz del Castillo, Memoirs, trans. Lockhart (1844)

segments.name: The King in His Father's House

stops.name: Tenochtitlan, the order against Cacamatzin
stops.date_confidence: Attested that Cacamatzin was arrested and brought to Tenochtitlan. The agency runs the other way from the version in circulation: Cortes ordered him to have it done, and he then sent troops to seize Cacamatzin in his palace. The initiative was not his and the motive is not established. The month orders the segment; he was not present at the arrest.
stops.campa: Cacamatzin, who owes him the Texcocan throne, is raising men to throw the Spaniards out. Cortes tells him to have his nephew arrested. He sends troops, and they take Cacamatzin inside his own palace while he is discussing the war with his captains, and bring him down to the lake and across it in a litter, into Tenochtitlan, where he is chained beside the uncle who put him on the Texcocan seat and has now taken him off it. Ixtlilxochitl, whom the same uncle passed over four years earlier, is not arrested. What the uncle wanted out of any of this is not recorded anywhere.
suggested_refs: The Acolhua resistance faction under Cacamatzin, broken by the arrest of early 1520

stops.name: The palace of Axayacatl, Cortes goes to the coast
stops.date_confidence: Narvaez landed on the Gulf coast in April 1520 and Cortes left Tenochtitlan to meet him, leaving Pedro de Alvarado in command of the garrison. The exact day of departure is not fixed here and the date orders the segment.
stops.campa: Panfilo de Narvaez lands near Cempoala with more men than Cortes has, sent from Cuba to arrest him. Cortes takes most of the garrison down to the coast to fight other Spaniards. The tlatoani now has two Spanish factions to read, one of them out of sight, and for the first time since November he is held by a man he has never dealt with. Pedro de Alvarado is left holding the city, the palace and the king with something like a hundred and twenty men.
suggested_refs: The defeat of Narvaez at Cempoala on 27 May 1520, which returned Cortes to the capital with a doubled force

stops.name: The sacred precinct, Toxcatl
stops.date_confidence: Dated 22 May 1520 by the worldhistory.org Tenochtitlan timeline; cortes.journey.json stages the same event on 20 May 1520. The two dates are not reconciled here. He was confined nearby and was not present.
stops.campa: The festival of Toxcatl is held with Alvarado's permission: the nobles and the singers and the dancers in the courtyard, unarmed, the image of Huitzilopochtli made of amaranth dough. Alvarado's men close the gates and kill everyone inside. Whatever he has been doing for six months, holding a city still while he calculates, stops working within the hour. The account in Book Twelve gives the order of it: the drummer first, then the hands, then the crowd pressed against the walls.
suggested_refs: Book XII of the Florentine Codex, whose Nahua account of the Toxcatl killing was compiled from survivors in Tlatelolco
The later Spanish proceedings against Pedro de Alvarado, in which testimony about the massacre was taken
sources: worldhistory.org, Tenochtitlan timeline, 'May 22, 1520 - The Toxcatl Massacre'
cortes.journey.json (which dates the same event 20 May 1520)

stops.name: The palace of Axayacatl, the siege
stops.date_confidence: Cortes returned to Tenochtitlan in the second half of June 1520 and the palace was besieged from his arrival. The day is approximate and orders the segment.
stops.campa: Cortes comes back with Narvaez's men folded into his own and finds the city shut: the market closed, the bridges lifted out of the causeways, the roofs full of people. The Mexica attack the palace and go on attacking it. Inside, the king is now openly what he has been in law since November, a prisoner of no use to anybody, whose authority the people outside have withdrawn. His brother Cuitlahuac is out there directing the assault, released by the Spaniards a few days earlier to reopen the market.
suggested_refs: Cuitlahuac, released to reopen the market and elected in his brother's place

stops.name: The palace of Axayacatl, the refusal
stops.date_confidence: Bernal Diaz, ch. CXXVI, reports the words at second hand, as what the king is said to have exclaimed; he did not hear them himself. The day is an ordering device and the sequence within 27-29 June is not fixed.
stops.campa: Cortes sends to ask him to go up and speak to his people and stop the attack. He refuses. Diaz has the refusal at second hand, as words the king is said to have exclaimed: that he is tired of life, and wishes never again to hear the name of the man asking him for anything. There is no politics in it at all. Diaz sets it down as two separate outbursts with a full sentence of narration standing between them, and the two halves have travelled ever since as one continuous speech.
stops.quote: Why does Malinche now turn to me?--to me, who am tired of life, and who could wish never again to hear his name mentioned, for it is he who has plunged me into all this misery! ... I will neither see nor hear anything more of this man. I put no longer any faith in his deceitful words, his promises, and his specious lies.
stops.quote_source: Bernal Diaz del Castillo, The Memoirs of the Conquistador Bernal Diaz del Castillo, trans. John Ingram Lockhart (London, 1844), vol. 1, ch. CXXVI, p. 344. Two utterances separated in the source by a sentence of narration, joined here by an ellipsis.
suggested_refs: Lockhart's 1844 translation, whose running heads fix this passage at p. 344 of vol. 1
sources: Bernal Diaz del Castillo, Memoirs, trans. Lockhart (1844), vol. 1, ch. CXXVI

stops.name: The palace of Axayacatl, Olmedo and Olid at the door
stops.date_confidence: Bernal Diaz, ch. CXXVI: father Olmedo and Olid went and spoke to him. The day is an ordering device.
stops.campa: The friar Bartolome de Olmedo and Cristobal de Olid go in and ask again. He agrees in the end, and before he goes he tells them plainly what he expects to happen. It is too late for any of it. The Mexica have already raised somebody else and will grant no truce whatever he says to them from a roof. He tells the friar and the captain that every one of them will die in this city, and he tells them this while agreeing to do the thing they came to ask for. Then he lets them take him up to the terrace.
stops.quote: Alas! for all this, it is now too late. I am convinced that the Mexicans, whatever my wishes might be, will not grant any cessation of arms... For myself, I am convinced you will every one of you meet with your death in this city.
stops.quote_source: Bernal Diaz del Castillo, The Memoirs of the Conquistador Bernal Diaz del Castillo, trans. John Ingram Lockhart (London, 1844), vol. 1, ch. CXXVI, p. 344. The ellipsis omits the middle clause naming the raising of another cazique.
suggested_refs: Bartolome de Olmedo, the Mercedarian friar attached to the expedition, and Cristobal de Olid
sources: Bernal Diaz del Castillo, Memoirs, trans. Lockhart (1844), vol. 1, ch. CXXVI

stops.name: The palace of Axayacatl, the terrace
stops.date_confidence: Bernal Diaz, ch. CXXVI, and the Noche Triste tradition. The quotation is the answer of four Mexica captains addressed to him and is not his own speech. The day is an ordering device and the internal sequence of 27-29 June is not fixed.
stops.campa: He goes up onto the terrace with Spanish shields held over him and speaks. Four captains come forward to a place where they can be heard, and answer him weeping, according to Diaz, and what they say is that they have already raised his cousin to the throne. Diaz names the cousin: Cuitlahuatzin, lord of Iztapalapa, his own brother. Then the stones and the darts come in past the shields, and he is hit on the head, the arm and the leg, and carried back down the stair into the palace.
stops.quote: Alas! great king, your own misfortune, and that of your children and your relatives, afflicts us sorely. But we dare not hide from you that we have raised one of your cousins to the throne of this country.
stops.quote_source: Bernal Diaz del Castillo, The Memoirs of the Conquistador Bernal Diaz del Castillo, trans. John Ingram Lockhart (London, 1844), vol. 1, ch. CXXVI, p. 345. The words of four Mexica captains addressed to him, not his own.
suggested_refs: The Spanish version of the fatal injuries, summarized on the PBS Conquistadors companion page
sources: Bernal Diaz del Castillo, Memoirs, trans. Lockhart (1844), vol. 1, ch. CXXVI

stops.name: Tenochtitlan, the death
stops.date_confidence: The 29 June date is conventional rather than proven; the death falls in the last days of June 1520. Cause and perpetrator are unresolved. Spanish accounts have him die of the stoning and of tearing off his bandages and refusing food; nearly all surviving indigenous-derived sources say the Spaniards stabbed or strangled him. Wikipedia gives his age as 48 or 49, indigenous chronicles as 52, a figure some scholars read as the length of the calendar cycle rather than a life. Coordinates are inherited byte-identical from the same event in cortes.journey.json, though the death occurred inside the palace pinned at 19.434, -99.1335 elsewhere in this file.
stops.campa: He dies inside the house of his father, three or four days after the stoning, and the manner of it is the one fact about him on which the two traditions of sources will never agree. The Spaniards say his own people killed him, and that he pulled the dressings off his wounds and refused food. The Nahua accounts say he was killed with a blade or a cord by the men holding him, along with the other lords in the room, on the eve of the escape. Both traditions were written down by people who needed the answer they gave.
suggested_refs: Matthew Restall, When Montezuma Met Cortes (2018), and its Spanish edition of 2019
The 2009 British Museum exhibition Moctezuma: Aztec Ruler and its accompanying BBC documentary
sources: Wikipedia, 'Moctezuma II' ('Death: June 29, 1520, in Tenochtitlan, aged 48-49')
Noticonquista (UNAM) on the indigenous age-at-death figure of 52
cortes.journey.json (coordinates and date of the same event)

stops.name: Tenochtitlan, the body carried out
stops.date_confidence: Attested in Bernal Diaz, ch. CXXVII, that the body was shown to the besiegers and that they answered with this cry. The quotation is theirs and not his. The day is an ordering device.
stops.campa: The Spaniards put the body where the besiegers can see it, on the theory that a dead king buys a truce. It buys nothing. The market stays shut and the bridges stay out of the causeways. What comes back over the wall is a demand: the Spaniards will pay for the death of their monarch and for the insult done to the gods, and they are invited to come out into the street and hear the terms in person. Seven months earlier this same crowd had lowered its eyes rather than look at him.
stops.quote: Now, we will make you pay dearly for the death of our monarch, and the insult you have offered to our gods! Is it now you beg peace of us? Only come out, and we will show you what terms we mean to make with you!
stops.quote_source: Bernal Diaz del Castillo, The Memoirs of the Conquistador Bernal Diaz del Castillo, trans. John Ingram Lockhart (London, 1844), vol. 1, ch. CXXVII, p. 347. The cry of Mexica warriors on seeing the body, not his own words.
suggested_refs: The election of Cuitlahuac, who ruled eighty days in the year 2 Flint and died in December 1520
sources: Bernal Diaz del Castillo, Memoirs, trans. Lockhart (1844), vol. 1, ch. CXXVII

stops.name: Copolco, the burning
stops.date_confidence: The cremation at Copolco is recorded in Book XII of the Florentine Codex, a Nahua account compiled decades after the event. Copolco's archaeological footprint is not fixed; the coordinate approximates the northern lake-edge district generally assigned to it, and a second value, 19.4361, -99.14, circulates for the same event in the research material. The day is an ordering device.
stops.campa: The body is released to the Mexica and taken to Copolco and burned. The account in Book Twelve says the people who stood watching it burn did not mourn him. They said he had been a tyrant, that he had terrorised his subjects and punished them unjustly, and that the fire crackled and roared. Nobody keeps the ash and there is no tomb. Copolco's own ground has never been fixed on a map, and two different coordinates circulate for the place where he burned.
suggested_refs: Book XII of the Florentine Codex, published complete and searchable by the Getty Research Institute in 2023
The featherwork headdress at the Weltmuseum Wien, held by tradition to be his, acquired by Austria from France in 1880 and the object of an unresolved Mexican repatriation campaign
sources: pbs.org, 'Conquistadors: Cortes' (removal and cremation of the body)
